growth_story.headline: Fiji's income per person stalled through a decade of coups and lost trade deals, then climbed to a new high on tourism despite the pandemic collapse.
growth_story.arc: Fiji's income per person grew 2.3 percent a year in 1990–1999, as the economy recovered from the 1987 coup and a garment industry grew up on trade deals with Australia, New Zealand and the United States. Growth then nearly stopped, at 0.2 percent a year in 2000–2009: coups in 2000 and 2006 drove out skilled people and business owners and hurt confidence, while garment trade deals and guaranteed European sugar prices came to an end. Since 2010 growth has averaged 2.6 percent a year, led by tourism, which the World Bank calls a major driver of activity in Fiji. That era also holds Fiji's sharpest swing: income per person fell 17.2 percent in 2020 and 4.5 percent in 2021 when borders closed, then rose 17.4 percent in 2022 and 8.9 percent in 2023 as visitors returned. By 2025 income per person was at its highest level yet, but growth swings more than in most economies, and the 2016–2025 average of 2.2 percent is only a little above the 1.8 percent of 2006–2015.

threads.title: Coups and lost confidence
threads.text: Fiji had coups in 1987, 2000 and 2006. The World Bank links each one to falling confidence and investment and to waves of skilled people leaving, and calls 2001–2010 a period of stagnation; income per person fell in 2000, 2007 and 2009.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: During the following 18 months, around 1,000 people left each month—most of them professionals and business owners.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: The emigration, loss of confidence, and strained international relations were exacerbated by the third coup in 2006.

threads.title: Trade preferences ran out
threads.text: Sugar and garments were both built on special access to rich-country markets: sugar on guaranteed prices in Europe, garments on trade deals with Australia, New Zealand and the United States. As those deals were phased out, the garment industry declined after 2000 and manufacturing began to shrink, in the same years as the flat 2000–2009 era.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: Manufacturing began to shrink in the early 2000s with the erosion of trade preferences.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: Since 2000, the garment industry has rapidly declined as trade preferences and tax concessions have been phased out.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: Systematic Country Diagnostic

threads.title: Tourism lifts and drops growth
threads.text: Tourism is now a large part of Fiji's economy, which ties income to visitor numbers. When borders shut in 2020 the economy collapsed, and when travel reopened it rebounded strongly in 2022, giving the largest yearly swings in income per person since 1961.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: 2023 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; and Staff Report
citations.quote: As a small island dependent on tourism, Fiji’s economy contracted sharply with the pandemic and then rebounded strongly in 2022

citations.title: Pacific Economic Update, May 2026
citations.quote: Fiji’s tourism sector comprises about one third of output and roughly one quarter of jobs

threads.title: Emigration and money sent home
threads.text: Skilled workers keep leaving, now often through Australian and New Zealand work schemes, which leaves gaps in tourism, health care and building. The money they send home has grown and supports household spending.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Fiji (October 2026)
citations.quote: As a result, labor shortages have intensified in tourism, healthcare, and construction, weighing on productivity and service delivery.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: 2023 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; and Staff Report
citations.quote: Buoyed by emigration and the rise of mobile money networks, remittances have doubled since 2017

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Fiji (October 2026)

threads.title: Cyclones and climate shocks
threads.text: Fiji sits in a cyclone belt. Cyclone Evan in 2012 slowed growth by hurting sugar output and tourist arrivals, and the World Bank still lists cyclones and droughts as a recurring threat to farms and infrastructure.

citations.title: Republic of Fiji: Systematic Country Diagnostic

since_last_year.text: Growth held up in 2025 on tourism, money sent home and government spending, with income per person up 2.7 percent. In 2026 the picture turned: higher oil prices raised living costs, and both the IMF and the World Bank now expect growth to slow this year.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Fiji
citations.quote: Growth is expected to fall in 2026 because of higher oil prices, softer tourism demand, and elevated uncertainty.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Fiji (October 2026)
citations.quote: Fiji’s post-COVID recovery is slowing as global energy shocks raise inflation and weaken growth to 2.1 percent in 2026

growth_story.tension: The World Bank's 2017 review, citing a 1995 IMF report, says investment failed to recover after the 1987 coup for lack of confidence. The data fit that up to the mid-1990s, with investment at 14.2 percent of GDP in 1995 against 12.5 percent in 1990. But investment then jumped to 26.0 percent in 1998, and income per person grew 2.3 percent a year over the decade.
